name: Prize crossword No 29,033
preamble: Some solutions may be entered backwards

clue.text: Put compost on a bin — alternatively, dig it in with this

blocks.note: to compost something is to let it rot down
taken as written
a vat is a large container or bin
'or' introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: Gardening advice: spread compost on a bin, or else work it into the soil with a tool.
explanation.walkthrough: In this palindrome-themed puzzle the answer reads the same both ways. 'Put compost' is taken as the verb sense, rot down.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotavator is a motorised machine with rotating blades used to break up soil and work material into the ground.

clue.text: Are their guts more developed?

indicators.note: something developed has grown into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the eight letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A playful question about whose stomachs are the most highly trained.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: people of refined appetite might be said to have more developed guts.
explanation.definitionFit: Gourmets are connoisseurs of fine food, so their palates and appetites are imagined as especially cultivated.

clue.text: Guitar player with the lowest sound

definitions.note: read as a mock superlative adjective, 'bass-est'

blocks.note: first meaning: someone who plays the bass guitar
second meaning: a jokey superlative of bass, the most bass

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one description of a musician; the second half is a punning superlative formed from the word for a low note.
explanation.definitionFit: A bassist plays the bass guitar, the instrument covering the deepest register in a rock band.

clue.text: Blasted palindrome left Soup put out — I’m sorry!

indicators.note: something blasted has been blown apart, so its letters scatter into a new order
to put something out is to eject it, so the named letters are removed

blocks.note: the word with L for left and I removed; Soup, the setter, is 'I'

explanation.surface: The setter apologises after an exploded palindrome has cast them out.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters refer to themselves by pseudonym, so Soup stands for 'I' here; L is the usual abbreviation for left.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are polite apologetic phrases said after a small social blunder, interchangeable in speech.

clue.text: I take position in firm round Barnet

indicators.note: to take a position inside something is to sit within it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: firm and hard both mean solid
taken as written
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: Someone joins a company located around the London district of Barnet.
explanation.walkthrough: Barnet looks like the London borough, but it is the definition: Cockney rhyming slang, Barnet Fair = hair.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a barnet is a person's hair or hairstyle, so it stands for a styled head of hair.

clue.text: Long stories drop top grades

blocks.note: to sag is to droop or drop
A is the top exam grade, so two or more are As

explanation.surface: Students' long essays cause their best marks to slip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drop' looks like a verb acting on the grades, but it supplies its own letters first.
explanation.definitionFit: A saga is a lengthy narrative, originally a Norse heroic tale, now any long involved story.

clue.text: Starsailor performances lacking support

definitions.note: a possessive name, Solo's, rather than a plural noun

blocks.note: first meaning: belonging to Han Solo, the Star Wars pilot who sails the stars
second meaning: pieces played or sung without accompaniment

explanation.surface: Gigs by the British rock band Starsailor fall flat without a backing act.
explanation.walkthrough: Starsailor is a real band, which makes it look like part of the scene; instead it points to the starship pilot Han Solo.
explanation.definitionFit: Unaccompanied pieces for a single performer have no backing musicians, which is what lacking support means.

clue.text: Pain — yes, like, on the tip of my tongue

indicators.note: a tip is the very end or point, so only the first letter is kept

blocks.note: mal is French for pain or illness, as in grand mal
ay is an old or dialect word for yes
à la means in the style of, or like
the first letter of this word

explanation.surface: Someone struggling for a word: it's painful, yes, like, right on the tip of my tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'on the tip of my tongue' splits: the first part selects a letter and 'tongue' alone is the definition, meaning language.
explanation.definitionFit: Malayalam is a Dravidian language spoken in the Indian state of Kerala; tongue is a standard synonym for language.

clue.text: Creatures which cut the mustard

indicators.note: a cut slices out a section, so the letters are taken from inside the words that follow

blocks.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: Animals that are up to the job, as in the idiom 'cut the mustard'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut the mustard' is an idiom for being good enough, which disguises the instruction to slice letters out.
explanation.definitionFit: Emus are large flightless Australian birds, so they are animals in the broadest sense of creatures.

clue.text: Food for sheep next to the sea in Portugal?

blocks.note: mar is the Portuguese word for sea
a ram is a male sheep

explanation.surface: A question about what sheep graze on along the Portuguese coast.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a loose definition: marram is a seaside grass, the sort of thing a sheep might graze.
explanation.definitionFit: Marram is a coarse grass binding coastal sand dunes, and grass is fodder for grazing animals.

clue.text: Football team comes second to another one involving stars

blocks.note: a side is a team
Real Madrid, another football team, often just called Real

explanation.surface: One club finishes runner-up to a rival in a league full of star players.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stars' sounds like famous footballers, but it means celestial bodies.
explanation.definitionFit: Sidereal means relating to the fixed stars, as in sidereal time measured against distant celestial bodies.

clue.text: Gently touches Chevrolet SS?

blocks.note: a Chevrolet is a make of car
the letter S spelt out, twice

explanation.surface: Fondly stroking a classic Chevrolet SS sports model.
explanation.walkthrough: SS is a real Chevrolet badge, so the surface makes sense; cryptically it is two letters written as words.
explanation.definitionFit: To caress is to stroke someone or something lightly and affectionately.

clue.text: When 12’s struck off totally?

definitions.note: read as two words, no 'on', an adjectival phrase

blocks.note: first meaning: the time of day when the clock strikes twelve
second meaning: split as a refusal plus the opposite of off, so not on at all

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the whimsical second sense: split the answer into two short words and it describes a switch with no 'on' whatsoever.
explanation.definitionFit: Midday is the hour at which a clock strikes twelve during daylight, and 'no on' means completely switched off.

clue.text: Thumps above the solar plexus

definitions.note: plural verb or noun for a singular noun

blocks.note: surface reading: punches landed on someone's upper body
setter's reading: the regular pulse of the organ sitting in the chest

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a boxing description of punches to the chest; really it is the body's own rhythmic thumping.
explanation.definitionFit: The pulse of the cardiac muscle is felt as a rhythmic pounding in the chest, just over the abdomen.

clue.text: First, they turn clay vessel

blocks.note: spinning tops are things that turn
a pot is a vessel made of clay

explanation.surface: A potter's instruction: first, they throw a clay vessel on the wheel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First' looks like a sequencing word opening the sentence, but it is the definition; 'they' are toys, not people.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in first place means occupying the highest position in a ranking, the number one slot.

clue.text: As instructed, nothing put on foundation that is not without substance

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase for an adjective

indicators.note: something without substance is hollow, so only its outside letters remain

blocks.note: O looks like zero
a bed is a base or foundation layer
i.e. abbreviates id est, 'that is'
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Doing what you're told: not applying makeup base that lacks real coverage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foundation' suggests cosmetics but means a base; 'not without substance' is not a double negative but a word emptied of its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: An obedient person does as they are told, complying with orders and directions given to them.

clue.text: Do work to prepare to hang new wall covering

indicators.note: to work something over is to rework it, so its letters get rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Decorating advice: put in the groundwork before hanging fresh wallpaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one long decorating instruction; the split is after the word that gets reworked.
explanation.definitionFit: Wallpaper is the usual wall covering, so putting up fresh wallpaper means doing the papering again.

clue.text: Rate rail disruption relating to a key part of the network

definitions.text: relating to a key part of the network

indicators.note: a disruption throws things out of their normal order

blocks.note: the eight letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Grading how badly rail delays affect a main line of the railway system.
explanation.walkthrough: The network seems to be railways, which makes the definition sit naturally in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An arterial road or line is a major route in a transport system, like an artery in the body's circulation.

clue.text: High arcs covering rear of stage that's essential for a Hamilton performance

definitions.text: that's essential for a Hamilton performance

indicators.note: someone high is intoxicated and wobbly, so the letters reel into a new order
to cover is to wrap round, so one piece sits inside the others
the rear is the back end, so only the last letter is kept

blocks.note: the plural read as two of the curves
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Soaring arcs spanning the back of the stage, vital for a show of the musical Hamilton.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamilton looks like the Broadway musical, but it is Lewis Hamilton, the Formula One driver; the answer reads the same in either direction.
explanation.definitionFit: A Formula One driver cannot compete without a vehicle built for motor racing, so it is essential to his performance.

clue.text: Loose iron shackles are beginning to be removed

indicators.note: to shackle is to bind around, so one piece is held inside another
removing the beginning means the first letter is dropped

blocks.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
the word without its first letter

explanation.surface: Taking off iron chains so a prisoner can go loose.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about removing shackles to set someone loose, which neatly matches the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something loose is unrestrained and at liberty, not tied or confined.

clue.text: More embarrassed about doctor describing the two early signs of dementia

indicators.note: to describe a shape is to draw round it, so one piece encircles another
the earliest signs are the opening letters, here the first pair

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
Dr is the abbreviation for doctor
the opening two letters of the word, taken as its first letters

explanation.surface: Someone grows more flustered as a doctor spots the first symptoms of dementia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Early signs' sounds medical, matching the doctor, but means opening letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Embarrassment makes the face flush, so a more embarrassed person is more flushed in colour.

clue.text: They review trips in a Quattro: not for everyone

indicators.note: U is the British film rating meaning suitable for all, so the universal letter is removed

blocks.note: the Quattro is a model made by Audi
tours, with one letter removed

explanation.surface: Inspectors examine journeys taken in an exclusive Audi Quattro.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a U certificate marks a film as suitable for everyone, so 'not for everyone' means take out U.
explanation.definitionFit: Auditors examine and check accounts formally, so they are people whose job is to review.

clue.text: Act finished: theatre stage cleared finally

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so each word gives its closing letter

blocks.note: the last letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: The curtain comes down on an act, and the stage is emptied.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Act' sits in a theatre picture as a division of a play, but it means a thing done.
explanation.definitionFit: A deed is something done, an action or achievement, just as an act is.

clue.text: Belief in infinite netherworld

indicators.note: the wanted word sits inside the following words

blocks.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: Faith in an endless underworld.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Belief in' reads as a phrase, but 'in' is doing a separate job pointing inside what follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenet is a principle or doctrine held as true by a group, a core article of faith.

clue.text: Something on the front page causing a bit of a frown?

blocks.note: first meaning: the big title above a newspaper story
second meaning: a crease on the forehead, read as two words

explanation.surface: A worrying news story on page one makes the reader frown.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as two words for the second sense: a wrinkle across the brow is part of a frown.
explanation.definitionFit: Newspapers print a large title over their main stories, and a frown leaves creases across the forehead.

clue.text: Clothe Nick in nurse's costume at last

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it
at last points to the end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: EN is an Enrolled Nurse
to nick is British slang for to steal or rob
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Finally dressing a man named Nick in a nurse's outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick looks like a man's name; it is the British slang verb meaning steal.
explanation.definitionFit: To enrobe is to dress someone in a robe or garment, a formal way of saying put clothes on.

clue.text: Note on private record reviewed every year

indicators.note: to review is to look back over, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: la is a note of the sol-fa scale
inner means private or personal
an EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A message attached to a confidential file that gets checked annually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Record' suggests a document, matching the private file, but it is a vinyl disc.
explanation.definitionFit: A perennial plant comes back season after season, lasting through many years, so it recurs annually.

clue.text: Married man’s wife’s address

blocks.note: m is the abbreviation for married
Adam, the first man in Genesis

explanation.surface: How a husband speaks to his wife.
explanation.walkthrough: It nods to the famous palindrome 'Madam, I'm Adam', the first man greeting his wife Eve.
explanation.definitionFit: Madam is a polite form of address to a woman, the way Adam is said to have greeted Eve.
